model: BVPS compounding x exit P/B (insurer/reinsurer holdco, dividends + terminal exit discounted at cost of equity)

inputs.wacc_rationale: Not a WACC engine -- Arch is a holding company earning underwriting profit and investment income; net debt (~$1.5-2B) is trivial relative to $24B of equity and is NOT deducted per the non-FCF-model rule (subtracting debt from an already-post-financing equity flow double counts it). Discount rate is cost of equity, built as ~4.3% 10yr UST + ~5.2pp equity risk premium adjusted for insurance-underwriting beta (~0.9-1.0), landing at 9.0-10.5% across scenarios.
inputs.lease_treatment: not applicable -- insurance holdco, no owner-FCF component build
inputs.nci_treatment: not applicable -- Arch has no material non-controlling interests; wholly owned subsidiaries
inputs.notes: MODEL CHOICE: Routed via .claude/skills/dcf-methods/SKILL.md row 'Insurer, holdco, compounder-of-book' -> BVPS compounding x exit P/B, matching the Fairfax (FRFHF) precedent in memory (frfhf-fairfax.md). An owner-FCF DCF is wrong for an insurer: operating cash flow is dominated by float movements and mark-to-market noise, EBITDA/EBIT are not meaningful for an underwriting business, and 'net debt' is trivial and not the balance sheet's story -- capital adequacy and underwriting leverage are. Instead the model compounds COMMON book value per share forward using ROE (net income / average common equity), nets out a small common dividend (~4% payout, consistent with Arch's historical near-nil common dividend policy -- the real capital return is buybacks), and treats share buybacks as retiring shares at a P/B that glides from the current 1.40x toward the assumed exit multiple. Terminal value = exit P/B x Year-5 BVPS; PV of interim per-share dividends is a rounding error (<$2/share across all scenarios) because virtually all capital return is via buyback, not dividend -- the per-share value creation shows up entirely in the compounding BVPS path and the terminal multiple, not in a dividend stream. Book value per share of $68.04 at Q2 2026 is Arch's own disclosed COMMON book value (excludes ~$298M of preferred equity implied by 24,030 GAAP equity minus 23,732 implied common equity at 68.04 x 348.8m shares -- reconciles cleanly, consistent with Arch's outstanding Series F preferred). Historical ROE: 16.3% (FY21), 11.2% (FY22, elevated cat losses), 28.4% (FY23, hard-market peak), 22.0% (FY24), 19.5% (FY25) -- base case starts at 16.5% for the remainder of FY2026/FY2027 and glides down to a mid-cycle 13% by Year 5 as property-cat reinsurance pricing softens (2026 mid-year renewals down up to 25% risk-adjusted per Analysis JSON), consistent with management's own 'cautious but opportunistic' framing. Buyback pace assumption (~$1.2B/quarter in Q2 2026, i.e. ~$4.8B annualized against ~$24B equity) is aggressive; base case tapers the fraction of retained earnings spent on buybacks from 75% to 60% as the cycle softens and capital needs for growth in casualty/mortgage segments compete for capital. Exit P/B: bear 1.00x (de-rate to tangible book as a soft market bites and reserve-development risk from social inflation crystallizes), base 1.35x (roughly in line with the current 1.40x, reflecting a normalized mid-cycle multiple for a diversified specialty (re)insurer with mortgage-segment ballast), bull 1.60x (re-rate on sustained high-teens ROE and continued Insurance/Reinsurance/Mortgage diversification premium, similar to peers like RenaissanceRe/Everest at cycle peaks).

historical_growth.growth_rate_source: equity_5yr_cagr (BVPS CAGR, most conservative of the three and the anchor for an insurer valued on book-value compounding)
historical_growth.growth_divergence_warning: Revenue (18.6%/5yr) and EPS (28.4%/5yr) both run well above BVPS growth (15.1%/5yr) because FY2023-2025 was a historic hard market (record combined ratios in the low-80s%) atop a much smaller premium base after the 2022 cat-loss trough; none of the three trailing CAGRs should be extrapolated forward given the explicit 2026 softening-cycle guidance in the Analysis JSON (property-cat rate-on-line down up to 25% at June 2026 renewals). Forward ROE/BVPS growth assumptions below are set materially below all three trailing CAGRs for this reason.

base.narrative: ROE glides from 16.5% (still-firm Reinsurance/Mortgage segments, Insurance absorbing elevated cat losses) to a mid-cycle 13% by Year 5 as 2026-2027 property-cat renewals reprice down; buyback pace tapers from ~75% to 60% of retained earnings as capital competes with organic growth in casualty and MidCorp/Entertainment; exit multiple 1.35x roughly matches today's 1.40x, i.e. no re-rating assumed, only compounding.

bull.narrative: Cat losses stay benign, casualty firming offsets property-cat softening, Mortgage segment remains a stable high-margin ballast, and disciplined cycle management (the core moat per Analysis JSON) keeps consolidated ROE in the mid-to-high teens through the horizon; sustained ROE justifies a re-rate to 1.60x book, in line with peer premium multiples (RenaissanceRe, Everest) at cycle peaks.

bear.narrative: Property-cat softening proves deeper and longer than guided (steepest decline since the late 1990s per Analysis JSON), adverse casualty reserve development from social inflation crystallizes, and a U.S. housing/employment downturn pressures the Mortgage segment simultaneously -- the diversification benefit fails to smooth the cycle in the way it has historically. ROE compresses to a high-single-digit/low-double-digit trough and the market de-rates the stock to roughly tangible book (1.00x) on capital-adequacy concerns.

sensitivity.sensitivity_note: Rows are cost of equity (%), columns are exit P/B multiple (x) -- an insurer's terminal value is driven by the exit book-value multiple, not a perpetuity growth rate, so 'terminal_growth_range' here holds the exit-P/B axis values for compatibility with the standard field name.

probability_weighted.weights_rationale: House default 25/50/25. Not skewed further toward bear despite the flagged softening reinsurance cycle, because Arch's Mortgage segment (12% of revenue, high-margin, credit-cycle rather than cat-cycle driven) and disciplined multi-segment capital rotation provide a demonstrated earnings floor through prior soft markets, and the balance sheet (~$27B capital, A+/A1-range ratings) carries no near-term solvency or refinancing risk that would justify a heavier bear weight.

valuation_philosophy.summary: Arch is valued as a book-value compounding machine, not a cash-flow-generating operating company. The three segments (Insurance, Reinsurance, Mortgage) earn underwriting profit plus investment income on float; that profit either gets paid out as a nominal common dividend (~4% payout -- Arch has historically preferred buybacks to dividends) or retained and compounded into book value, with a further layer of per-share value creation from buying back stock below its eventual exit multiple. The model therefore projects common BVPS forward year by year from ROE and the buyback-funded share count, and prices the business as the present value of (small) interim dividends plus a Year-5 exit at an assumed price-to-book multiple, discounted at the cost of equity. This mirrors the Fairfax Financial (FRFHF) precedent in the user's memory and is the correct family of model per the dcf-methods routing table's 'Insurer, holdco, compounder-of-book' row.
key_risks_to_valuation: Property-catastrophe reinsurance pricing is softening sharply into 2026-2027 renewals (up to 25% risk-adjusted rate-on-line decline at June 2026), which could push ROE below even the bear case if it proves structural rather than cyclical

Casualty reserve adequacy is a live industry-wide risk from social inflation and nuclear jury verdicts; a reserve charge would hit book value directly and is not distinguishable in this model from a bad underwriting year

The exit P/B assumption does almost all the work (>98% of intrinsic value in every scenario comes from the terminal exit price, not interim dividends) because Arch pays a nominal common dividend -- the valuation is highly sensitive to the multiple the market is willing to pay for book value in five years, which is a market-sentiment variable this model cannot forecast with precision

Buyback-price assumptions (glide from 1.40x to the exit multiple) are a modeling simplification; if Arch continues repurchasing well above or below that glide path, the actual share count and per-share compounding will differ

Mortgage segment (GSE-linked) carries external policy risk (PMIERs, FHFA/GSE reform, increased use of credit risk transfer) that is outside Arch's control and could remove the segment's diversification benefit
